subtopics.name: Stack simulation & bracket matching
subtopics.summary: A stack (LIFO) processes the most recent unfinished item first. It shows up in bracket/parenthesis sequences, undo operations, "collapse adjacent equal/opposite items" simulations and expression parsing. Recognise it when an element only interacts with the latest still-open element.
learn: std::stack / vector push_back+pop_back; check empty() before top()/pop()
Regular bracket sequence: balance never negative and ends at 0; match each ")" with the stack top
Collapse simulations (remove adjacent pairs, colliding objects) are a stack scan in O(n)
Store indices, not values, on the stack so you can measure lengths/distances (longest valid substring)
Process collisions/annihilations by grouping (e.g. by parity) and matching with a stack
Every element is pushed and popped at most once -> amortised O(n)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Data Structures

problems.name: Replace To Make Regular Bracket Sequence

subtopics.name: Monotonic stack / nearest smaller values
subtopics.summary: Keep a stack whose values are monotone; when a new element arrives, pop everything it "beats". This gives, for every index, the nearest smaller/greater element to the left/right in O(n). It appears in largest-rectangle, "sum over all subarrays of max/min", visibility/jump and contribution-counting problems.
learn: Nearest smaller to the left: pop while top >= a[i]; the remaining top is the answer
Run it left-to-right and right-to-left to get the span [L_i, R_i] where a[i] is the minimum/maximum
Contribution technique: sum of max over all subarrays = sum a[i]*(i-L_i)*(R_i-i); break ties with < on one side and <= on the other
Largest rectangle in histogram and maximal all-ones sub-rectangle (row-by-row histograms)
Stack + DP: dp[i] computed from the element popped / the new top (skyscrapers, skyline, jumps)
Count "rounds until stable" style processes (Psychos in a line) with stack-stored step counts
The same stack pass builds the Cartesian tree (parent = the larger of the nearest smaller neighbours) - see the Cartesian tree sub-topic

subtopics.name: Queues & deques (simulation)
subtopics.summary: A queue (FIFO) serves items in arrival order; a deque allows push/pop at both ends. They are used for round-based simulations, BFS, rotating sequences and greedy constructions that append to the front or back.
learn: std::queue for FIFO simulation; std::deque supports push/pop_front/back and random access in O(1)
Rotations: pop_front then push_back simulates a cyclic shift; detect when the process becomes periodic
Greedy deque building: decide per element whether it goes to the front or back
Keep a set/array of "currently in the queue" flags to avoid duplicates
Bound the number of simulation steps (or detect cycles) before brute-forcing

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Data Structures

subtopics.name: Monotonic deque / sliding window min-max
subtopics.summary: A deque kept monotone gives the minimum/maximum of every window of a sliding range in amortised O(1). It speeds up DPs of the form dp[i] = min(dp[j]) + cost over j in a window, and two-pointer problems that need the window extreme.
learn: Push back after popping worse elements from the back; pop front when the index leaves the window
Store indices in the deque, not values
Sliding window DP: dp[i] = min_{i-k<=j<i} dp[j] + c_i in O(n) instead of O(nk)
Two pointers with window max-min <= K: two deques (one for max, one for min)
Min-queue from two min-stacks: push onto the in-stack, pop from the out-stack (refill by moving everything when empty) - works for any associative op, e.g. gcd
Alternative: a queue built from two min-stacks, or a multiset when you also need deletions by value
Sliding median/cost needs two multisets (or order statistics), not a deque

subtopics.name: Linked lists (array-based) & deletions
subtopics.summary: Doubly linked lists stored in prev[]/next[] arrays allow O(1) deletion of an element while keeping neighbours. They are the tool for "repeatedly delete elements and look at the new neighbours" simulations, often combined with a set/priority queue of candidates.
learn: nxt[i], prv[i] arrays; deleting i: nxt[prv[i]] = nxt[i], prv[nxt[i]] = prv[i]
Use sentinels 0 and n+1 to avoid boundary checks
Only the neighbours of deleted elements change -> re-check only them each round (amortised O(n))
Combine with a std::set / priority_queue of "active" candidates (largest, closest, ...)
Josephus-type problems: linked list for small n, order-statistics tree/BIT for large n
std::list exists but array-based lists are faster and easier to index

resources.title: USACO Guide: More Operations on Sorted Sets (combine with sets)

subtopics.name: Cartesian tree & divide-and-conquer on the maximum
subtopics.summary: The Cartesian tree of an array has the maximum (or minimum) at the root and the left/right parts as subtrees; it is built in O(n) with a monotonic stack. Problems that recurse "split at the maximum, solve both sides" or count subarrays whose max/min sits at a given index are DP or counting on this tree, often combined with iterating over the smaller side.
learn: Build with one stack pass: pop smaller elements, the last popped becomes the left child, the new element becomes the right child of the stack top
Node i owns the range (L_i, R_i) between its nearest greater elements; subtree = that range
Recursion f(l, r) = solve(l, m-1) + solve(m+1, r) with m = argmax via sparse table is the same tree, built top-down
Iterate over the smaller of the two sides at each node: total O(n log n) (special segments, max = sum conditions)
Tree DP on the Cartesian tree counts arrays with a given "position of maximum" structure
Offline queries on the recursion (f(l, r)) become sums over nearest-greater spans with a BIT sweep

cp-algorithms: Treap (Cartesian tree), building in O(n)

problems.name: Max to the Right of Min

subtopics.name: Sets & maps basics (counting, distinct)
subtopics.summary: std::set keeps distinct sorted keys, std::map associates a value with each key (frequency counts, last positions, id->name). These solve "have I seen this?", "how many times?" and "group equal things" questions in O(log n).
learn: set.insert/erase/count/find in O(log n); size() gives the number of distinct elements
map<key,int> cnt; cnt[x]++ for frequencies; iterate in sorted order of keys
Group by a normalised key: pair of reduced ratio, difference a_i - i, sorted string, etc.
Count pairs with equal key: for each element add cnt[key] before inserting
Use map<long long,...> when keys exceed int; beware operator[] inserting default values

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Sets & Maps

subtopics.name: Hash maps & anti-hash tests
subtopics.summary: unordered_map/unordered_set give expected O(1) lookups, but on Codeforces they can be hacked with keys that all collide, giving O(n^2) and TLE. Know when to use them, how to make them safe (custom random hash), or simply fall back to map / sorting.
learn: Default std::hash for integers is identity -> adversarial inputs (multiples of a bucket prime) blow up unordered_map
Fix: custom hash with splitmix64 + a random seed from chrono; or gp_hash_table with a custom hash
Call reserve() to avoid rehashing; avoid unordered_map for pair keys without a good hash
Often a sorted vector + binary search or coordinate compression is both safer and faster
Typical uses: count equal prefix sums / pairs with given difference (a_i - i), sum of k values (meet in the middle)

resources.title: Blowing up unordered_map, and how to stop getting hacked on it (neal)

subtopics.name: Priority queues / heaps
subtopics.summary: A binary heap returns the current largest (or smallest) element in O(log n). It powers greedy algorithms that repeatedly take the best available option, "regret" greedies that undo the worst earlier choice, event simulation and Dijkstra.
learn: priority_queue<T> is a max-heap; use greater<T> or push negatives for a min-heap
Greedy with regret: take everything, and when a constraint breaks pop the worst taken item
Process items sorted by one key while a heap holds the best candidates by another key
Merge k sorted lists / k smallest sums with a heap of frontier states
Lazy deletion: keep a "deleted" marker or a second heap instead of erasing from the middle
Marginal-gain greedy: push the improvement of splitting/upgrading an item, always take the largest

subtopics.name: Ordered sets & multisets (lower_bound tricks)
subtopics.summary: Sorted containers support "smallest element >= x", "largest element < x", deleting one copy and iterating neighbours, all in O(log n). They solve matching/assignment greedies, dynamic nearest-neighbour queries and maintaining the max gap or the median.
learn: s.lower_bound(x) / upper_bound(x); prev(it) for the largest element < x; check it != begin()/end()
Use the member s.lower_bound, never std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end()) (that is O(n))
multiset::erase(value) removes ALL copies; erase(s.find(value)) removes one
Maintain gaps between consecutive points: on insert/delete update a multiset of differences
Greedy matching: for each item take the smallest available partner >= need and erase it
Two multisets (low/high halves) keep the median / sum of k smallest under insertions and deletions
map<int,int> of position -> value for sparse arrays and "next occurrence" queries

resources.title: USACO Guide: More Operations on Sorted Sets
USACO Guide: (Optional) Sorted Sets with Custom Comparators

subtopics.name: Maintaining disjoint intervals in a set (ODT / Chtholly)
subtopics.summary: Store a partition of the line into maximal segments with the same value in a std::set/map keyed by left endpoint. Range-assign operations split at l and r and merge everything in between, giving amortised O((n+q) log n). Also covers "skip already-processed positions" with a set of alive indices.
learn: split(pos): find the segment containing pos and cut it into [l,pos-1] and [pos,r]; always split(r+1) before split(l)
Assign on [l,r]: split, erase all segments inside, insert one new segment -> number of segments stays amortised small
Chtholly tree (ODT) complexity relies on random/assign-heavy queries; do not use it when there are no assignments
Set of unprocessed indices: repeatedly s.lower_bound(l) and erase until > r -> each index removed once
Combine with a BIT to add contributions per removed/merged segment (colorful operations)

resources.title: USACO Guide: More Operations on Sorted Sets
Codeforces Round #449 editorial (problem 896C, origin of the Chtholly tree / ODT)

subtopics.name: Order-statistics tree (pb_ds) & inversion counting
subtopics.summary: GNU pb_ds tree with tree_order_statistics_node_update is a set that also answers find_by_order(k) (k-th smallest) and order_of_key(x) (# elements < x) in O(log n). It replaces a BIT in counting inversions, ranks, dynamic medians and Josephus-style deletions.
learn: #include <ext/pb_ds/assoc_container.hpp>; typedef tree<T, null_type, less<T>, rb_tree_tag, tree_order_statistics_node_update> ordered_set
For a multiset store pair(value, unique id) or use less_equal (but erase is then broken)
Inversions (distinct values): before inserting a_i, the number of earlier elements greater than a_i is (count inserted so far) - order_of_key(a_i + 1)
k-th alive element after deletions (Josephus, list removals)
Same queries can be done with a BIT over compressed values (often faster and safer)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Point Update Range Sum (Order Statistic Tree section)
C++ STL: Policy based data structures

subtopics.name: Prefix sums, 2D prefix sums & difference arrays
subtopics.summary: Prefix sums answer range-sum queries on a static array in O(1); difference arrays apply many range additions offline in O(1) each and recover the array with one prefix sum. 2D versions handle sub-rectangle sums. Recognise them whenever queries/updates are on ranges and the array does not change between queries.
learn: pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i]; sum(l,r) = pre[r] - pre[l-1]; use long long
Difference array: d[l] += x, d[r+1] -= x, then prefix-sum d
Count operations applied to each operation (difference array on the operations themselves)
2D: P[i][j] = a + P[i-1][j] + P[i][j-1] - P[i-1][j-1]; rectangle by inclusion-exclusion
Prefix sums + hashmap/count to count subarrays with sum k or sum divisible by m
Prefix counts per value/bit (per-letter, per-bit prefix arrays) for frequency-on-range queries

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Prefix Sums
USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums

subtopics.name: Sparse table / RMQ (idempotent queries)
subtopics.summary: A sparse table precomputes answers on all power-of-two-length ranges in O(n log n) and answers min/max/gcd/and/or queries in O(1) by overlapping two blocks. Use it for static arrays with many queries, frequently together with binary search or two pointers.
learn: st[k][i] = op(st[k-1][i], st[k-1][i + 2^(k-1)]); query with k = __lg(r-l+1)
O(1) queries only for idempotent operations (min, max, gcd, and, or); sum needs O(log n) or prefix sums
Binary search on the answer + RMQ: longest subarray with gcd > 1, max - min <= k, etc.
gcd/and/or over subarrays starting at i take only O(log V) distinct values
Disjoint sparse table / divide-and-conquer answers any associative op in O(1) (USACO Plat DC-SRQ)
Memory n log n: use int, and arrange as st[k][i] for cache efficiency

subtopics.name: Fenwick tree: point update, prefix query, inversions
subtopics.summary: A binary indexed tree supports adding to a position and querying a prefix sum in O(log n) with ~10 lines of code. With coordinate compression it counts elements less than x seen so far, which solves inversion counting and many "count pairs i<j with condition" problems.
learn: update: for(; i<=n; i += i&-i); query: for(; i>0; i -= i&-i); 1-indexed!
Range sum = query(r) - query(l-1); works for any invertible operation (sum, xor)
Coordinate-compress values first (sort + unique + lower_bound)
Count pairs i<j with a_j < a_i (inversions) / with prefix-sum conditions by sweeping and querying the BIT
Sort by one coordinate and use the BIT for the other (2D dominance counting, nested segments)
Prefix max BIT works only when values only increase

resources.title: USACO Guide: Point Update Range Sum

subtopics.name: BIT range updates & binary lifting (k-th element)
subtopics.summary: Storing the difference array in a BIT gives range-add / point-query; two BITs give range-add / range-sum. Descending the BIT bit by bit finds the smallest prefix whose sum reaches k in O(log n), i.e. the k-th smallest element of a multiset of values.
learn: Range add, point query: add(l, x), add(r+1, -x); value = prefix(i)
Range add, range sum: two BITs B1, B2 with sum(i) = B1(i)*i - B2(i)
k-th one / k-th smallest: walk pos from the highest power of two, skipping blocks whose sum < k
Offline sorting of queries + BIT k-th answers "k-th element among the first m" queries
Euler tour + range-add BIT gives subtree updates / path-to-root point queries on trees

resources.title: USACO Guide: Range Update Range Query

subtopics.name: 2D BIT & 2D offline counting
subtopics.summary: A Fenwick tree of Fenwick trees answers point-update / rectangle-sum queries in O(log^2 n) for moderate grids. For large coordinates the standard alternative is offline: sweep one dimension and keep a 1D BIT over the other, or use a BIT of sorted vectors / ordered sets.
learn: update(x,y): nested loops over x += x&-x and y += y&-y; rectangle by inclusion-exclusion
Memory n*m: only feasible for ~1000x1000 (or with bitsets/xor tricks)
Offline 2D dominance: sort points and queries by x, sweep with a BIT on y
Range-update range-query in 2D needs 4 BITs (xor variants need parity tricks)
Large coordinates online: BIT of sorted vectors (offline-known coordinates) or sqrt decomposition

subtopics.name: Segment tree: point update, range query
subtopics.summary: A segment tree stores an associative aggregate (sum, min, max, gcd, ...) for O(n) canonical segments, so point updates and range queries cost O(log n). It is the general-purpose range-query structure used whenever the array changes between queries or the operation is not invertible.
learn: Size 4n recursive or 2n iterative (bottom-up) implementation; know both
Node stores the aggregate of its segment; combine children with the associative operation
Store extra info per node: (min, count of min), (gcd, count equal to gcd), bitmask of letters
Alternating operations per level (Xenia) — node operation can depend on depth
Build in O(n); check the identity element for empty ranges (0 for sum, INF for min)
If only prefix sums are needed and values are invertible, a BIT is shorter

resources.title: USACO Guide: Point Update Range Sum

subtopics.name: Segment tree with custom node merge
subtopics.summary: Many problems need nodes that store several values merged non-trivially: max subarray sum (sum, best prefix, best suffix, best), bracket matching (unmatched open/close), sorted runs (prefix/suffix length), or a small DP/matrix whose merge is matrix multiplication. Design the node so that merge(left,right) is associative.
learn: Max subarray: node = {sum, pref, suf, best}; merge in O(1)
Brackets: node = {matched, open, close}; matched += min(left.open, right.close)
Non-commutative merges: keep order left-then-right; iterative trees need separate left/right accumulators
Counting non-decreasing subarrays: store length, prefix run, suffix run, count
Small DP state per node (e.g. 3x3 or 5x5 automaton matrix) merged by (min,+) matrix product
Write merge once and reuse it for both build/update and query

resources.title: USACO Guide: More Applications of Segment Tree (non-commutative combiners)
cp-algorithms: Segment Tree (finding subsegments with maximal sum)

subtopics.name: Walking / descending on a segment tree
subtopics.summary: Instead of binary searching outside the tree (O(log^2 n)), descend from the root choosing the child that still contains the answer, in O(log n). This finds the k-th one, the first index with a_i >= x, the first position where a prefix sum exceeds a value, or the leftmost element in [l, r] not divisible by g.
learn: k-th one: if left.count >= k go left else k -= left.count and go right
First index >= l with a_i >= x: recursive search that skips nodes with max < x
Combine walks with range restrictions by visiting only O(log n) canonical nodes
Find max suffix with positive sum (matching problems like Serge and Dining Room)
Interactive / offline variants: cache node counts to reuse queries

resources.title: USACO Guide: More Applications of Segment Tree (walking)
cp-algorithms: Segment Tree (searching for the k-th zero / first element greater than x)

problems.name: Bash and a Tough Math Puzzle

subtopics.name: Lazy propagation (range update, range query)
subtopics.summary: Lazy propagation postpones range updates by storing a pending tag in each node and pushing it to children only when needed, so both range updates and range queries cost O(log n). Common tags: range add, range assign, range flip/xor per bit, multiply, and combinations of them.
learn: Each node: aggregate + lazy tag; push(node) before descending; pull(node) after recursing
Compose tags correctly: assign overrides add; (mul, add) composes as an affine map
Range xor / flip: store per-bit counts (count of ones in each of ~20 bits)
Euler tour turns subtree updates on trees into range updates
Range add + range min/max is the most common combo (max overlap of intervals, dp with ranges)
26 lazy trees (one per letter) or counting sort per range for string range-sort problems

resources.title: USACO Guide: Range Update Range Query
cp-algorithms: Segment Tree (range updates / lazy propagation)

subtopics.name: Coordinate compression & dynamic (sparse) segment trees
subtopics.summary: When indices are huge (up to 1e9) either compress the coordinates offline or create nodes on demand (dynamic segment tree, O(q log C) nodes). A very common pattern is a segment tree indexed by value or prefix-sum, used to speed up DP transitions dp[i] = best over j with some key condition.
learn: Offline: collect all coordinates/queries, sort+unique, map to 0..m-1
Dynamic tree: children created lazily (pointer or index arrays), root covers [0, C)
Segment tree over values for dp[i] = max over earlier j with key_j < key_i (LIS-like)
Segment tree over prefix sums for dp with sign conditions (sum > 0, sum = 0)
Careful with interval endpoints when compressing ranges (compress l and r+1)

subtopics.name: Merge sort tree & wavelet ideas
subtopics.summary: Each segment-tree node stores the sorted list of its segment (or another structure such as a BIT/set). A query splits into O(log n) nodes and binary searches each, answering "how many values in a[l..r] are <= x" in O(log^2 n) online. Wavelet trees and persistent trees are faster alternatives for the same k-th / count queries.
learn: Build by merging children: O(n log n) memory and time
Count values < x in [l, r]: sum of lower_bound over O(log n) nodes
k-th smallest in range: binary search on the answer with the count query (O(log^3)) or use persistent/wavelet tree
Node can hold any structure (set, BIT, convex hull) -> "segment tree of X"
Fractional cascading reduces queries to O(log n) (rarely needed)

resources.title: CPH: Data structures (segment tree nodes containing structures)
cp-algorithms: Segment Tree (saving the entire subarrays in each vertex)

subtopics.name: Persistent segment tree
subtopics.summary: A persistent segment tree copies only the O(log n) nodes changed by each update, keeping every past version. Building versions over prefixes of the array answers k-th smallest in a range, distinct values in a range and "count of x in [l,r] among elements <= v" online in O(log n).
learn: Node pool with left/right child indices; update returns a new root
Version i = tree after inserting a_1..a_i; query(l,r) uses root[r] minus root[l-1]
k-th smallest in [l,r]: descend both versions simultaneously comparing count differences
Online distinct-in-range: version r marks only the last occurrence of each value
Memory: each update creates ~log2(n)+1 nodes, so allocate about (n + q) * 20 nodes (20-40 x n) statically
Version trees (undo/rollback queries) can also be handled offline by DFS over the version tree

subtopics.name: Segment tree beats & amortised segment trees
subtopics.summary: Some range updates (a_i %= x, a_i = sqrt(a_i), a_i = min(a_i, x), a_i = d(a_i)) cannot be lazily tagged but each element can change only a few times, or changes collapse values together. Recursing until a node is "settled" gives amortised O((n+q) log n) or O(n log^2 n) — the idea behind segment tree beats (Ji driver segtree).
learn: Range mod / sqrt / divisor-count: skip a node if max < x (or all values <= 2); each element changes O(log) times
Chmin beats: store max, second max and count of max; tag only when second_max < x < max
Potential-function argument: total work bounded by number of value changes
Range assign with color-merging amortisation (segments of equal colour)
Very advanced (beats with history sums) rarely needed below 2600

resources.title: A simple introduction to "Segment tree beats" (jiry_2)

topics.name: Offline Queries, Sweep Line & Sqrt Techniques

subtopics.name: Offline queries & sweep line with BIT/segment tree
subtopics.summary: If all queries are known in advance, sort them (by right endpoint, by x-coordinate, by time) and sweep, maintaining a BIT/segment tree/set that answers each query when the sweep reaches it. Classic: distinct values in a range (keep only the last occurrence), counting nested/intersecting segments, events of intervals.
learn: Event sweep: +1 at l, -1 at r+1, sort events (tie-breaking matters!) to get max overlap/covered points
Distinct in [l,r]: sort queries by r; when a value reappears clear its previous position in the BIT
Count points in rectangles / segments containing points: sort by one coordinate, BIT on the other
Answer queries in reverse (deletions become insertions) when that is easier
Process segments sorted by left endpoint while a set holds open segments (union of intervals, building graphs)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Range Queries with Sweep Line
USACO Guide: More Applications of Segment Tree

subtopics.name: Sqrt decomposition (blocks, heavy/light, batching)
subtopics.summary: Split the array into ~sqrt(n) blocks storing aggregates, so updates and queries touch O(sqrt n) blocks/elements. The same idea appears as "small parameter -> precompute, large parameter -> brute force" (threshold on step size or set size) and as rebuilding a structure every sqrt(q) queries.
learn: Blocks of size B ~ sqrt(n): full blocks via aggregate, partial blocks element by element
Threshold trick: for step k <= sqrt(n) precompute answers, for k > sqrt(n) only n/k terms exist
Heavy/light sets: sets larger than sqrt(total) are few, handle them specially
Batching/rebuilding: keep a buffer of recent updates and rebuild every sqrt(q) operations
Tune B empirically; prefer cache-friendly arrays; sqrt solutions often run near the time limit

subtopics.name: Mo's algorithm
subtopics.summary: Mo's algorithm answers offline range queries by sorting them in blocks of the left endpoint and moving two pointers, with O(1) or O(log) add/remove operations, for total O((n + q) sqrt n). It is the go-to tool for 'number of distinct / pairs with property / frequency-based value in [l, r]' when no clever sweep exists.
learn: Sort by (l / B, r), alternating r direction per block (odd-even trick) for speed; B ~ n / sqrt(q)
Implement add(i) and remove(i) that update a global answer and frequency array
Prefix xors turn "subarrays with xor k" into pairs of prefix indices inside the range
Mo's on trees: Euler tour (in/out times) to linearise paths or subtrees
Mo's with updates: add a time dimension, block size n^(2/3), complexity O(n^(5/3))
Hilbert-curve ordering is a faster alternative ordering

resources.title: USACO Guide: Square Root Decomposition (Mo's algorithm)
An alternative sorting order for Mo's algorithm (Hilbert order)

subtopics.name: Small-to-large merging (DSU on tree)
subtopics.summary: When merging sets/maps, always insert the smaller one into the larger one: each element moves O(log n) times, so total work is O(n log^2 n) with std::set/map. On trees this computes per-subtree statistics (dominant colour, counts per depth) by merging children into the heaviest child.
learn: swap(a, b) if a.size() < b.size(), then insert b into a (swap of std containers is O(1))
Tree version (sack): keep the heavy child data, re-add light subtrees
Maintain auxiliary aggregates (max frequency, sum of dominant colours) during insertion
Also works for merging DSU components with lists and for merging priority queues
Alternative linear-time approaches: Euler tour + offline sweep, or long-path decomposition for depth-indexed data
Segment-tree merging (merging dynamic segment trees of children in total O(n log n)) is the faster cousin for value-indexed data

subtopics.name: Parallel binary search
subtopics.summary: When every query needs its own binary search over time ("first moment when condition holds"), and each check requires replaying the same sequence of updates, run all binary searches simultaneously: in each of O(log T) rounds sort queries by their midpoint, replay the updates once and check every query as the replay passes its midpoint. Total O((T + Q) log T * cost of update).
learn: Recognise: answer for each query is monotone in time / in a threshold, and checking one time costs a full replay of updates
Per round: bucket queries by mid = (lo + hi) / 2, reset the structure, apply updates 1..T in order and test queries in bucket t after update t
Usual structures inside: DSU (first time u and v are connected), BIT with range add (meteor-style accumulation), segment tree
O(log T) rounds; reset the structure each round (DSU re-init, BIT clear)
Alternatives to compare: persistent structures, Kruskal reconstruction tree, divide and conquer over time with rollback
Recursive form: solve(lo, hi, queries) applies updates of [lo, mid], splits queries into two lists and recurses (needs undo or careful order)

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Binary search (Parallel Binary Search section)

subtopics.name: Offline deletion / segment tree over time
subtopics.summary: If a structure supports insertions and rollback (undo) but not deletions — like DSU without path compression or a linear basis — place each element on the O(log q) segment-tree nodes covering its lifetime in the query timeline, then DFS the tree applying and undoing insertions. This gives offline dynamic connectivity and similar results in O(q log q * T).
learn: Each element is alive on a time interval [add, remove); add it to O(log q) canonical nodes
DFS the time segment tree: apply node items on entry, answer leaf queries, roll back on exit
DSU with union by size and no path compression supports O(log n) rollback via a change stack
Works for any "insert + undo" structure: DSU, xor basis, knapsack dp array
Divide-and-conquer on queries (CDQ, see @dc-cdq) is the related technique for offline insertions + queries
Knapsack variant: items alive on time intervals, or "take a whole array except one" (1442D) - add items to segment-tree nodes and copy the dp array on the way down

subtopics.name: Treaps & implicit treaps (split/merge)
subtopics.summary: A treap is a randomised balanced BST supporting split and merge in expected O(log n). Keyed by implicit position, it becomes a dynamic array supporting cut-and-paste of subarrays, reversals (with a lazy flag), insertions in the middle and range aggregates — things a segment tree cannot do.
learn: Node: key/size, random priority, left/right, aggregate, lazy tags
split(t, k) into first k elements and the rest (implicit key = size of left subtree)
merge(l, r) assumes all of l is before r; choose the root by priority
Cut-and-paste and reversal: split into three parts, modify/flag the middle, merge back
Push lazy tags (reverse, add) before split/merge; recompute size and aggregate after
Alternatives: rope (__gnu_cxx::rope) or sqrt decomposition for some problems
